Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress
I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

vignette:
Anjali, a 25-year-old database administrator, presented for treatment six months after a severe motor vehicle collision. She described a life that had shrunk to the four walls of her apartment and the predictable logic of her computer screen, a stark contrast to the vibrant social life she had enjoyed with her husband before the accident. The event itself remained a series of searingly vivid, fragmented images. She had been driving, with her best friend, Priya, in the passenger seat. They were in the middle of a heated, albeit trivial, argument about weekend plans when a truck ran a red light. Anjali remembers the screech of tires, the force of the impact that threw her against the steering wheel, and then turning to see Priya unconscious and bleeding.

In the months that followed, the world became a minefield of reminders. The most potent trigger was Priya’s name; hearing it on television or in passing conversation would cause a jolt of panic, as if the accident were happening all over again. This sensitivity to specific names, coupled with a newfound terror of conflict, began to dictate her behaviour. Any disagreement, even a minor one with her husband, felt catastrophic. It would instantly activate a profound and unshakeable sense of self-blame. In her mind, the logic was inescapable: their argument in the car had distracted her, and that distraction was why she hadn't reacted a split-second sooner. The belief that the event happened "because of the way I acted" became the central organizing principle of her distress.

This conviction that she was fundamentally at fault drove her to withdraw from the people who might have offered comfort. The guilt she felt over Priya’s injuries, which were severe, was a constant, heavy presence. She came to believe she would never forgive herself for not doing more, and this appraisal fueled a deep avoidance of her social circle. Invitations from friends, especially those she shared with Priya, went unanswered. She knew they would ask about the accident, and she was certain she would see condemnation in their eyes. This avoidance of friends only served to reinforce her negative beliefs; her isolation felt like a just punishment, proof that she was the unforgivable person she believed herself to be. Her world became smaller, and her sense of mistrust grew—if she couldn't even trust herself to keep her best friend safe, then no one, and nothing, could truly be relied upon.

The maintenance cycle is now deeply entrenched. A trigger, such as her husband raising his voice in frustration over her withdrawal, not only brings back the memory but also her core belief: "This is my fault." This appraisal, in turn, dictates her strategy. Rather than engage, she flees, shutting herself in the bedroom to avoid the escalating stress. This pattern of avoiding any situation that puts her body under stress, including the physiological arousal of an argument, has become her default. Her work as a database administrator, once a source of satisfaction, now presents its own threats. The uncertainty of a complex project or a tight deadline mirrors the terrifying unpredictability of the accident, triggering a cascade of anxiety and prompting her to avoid challenging new assignments. This professional retreat has begun to strain her relationship with her manager, adding another layer of consequence to her shrinking world.

When the weight of these thoughts becomes too much to bear, Anjali resorts to a more desperate strategy. The feeling of being trapped by her own guilt leads her to self-harm, digging her nails into the skin of her arms until the sharp, physical pain provides a momentary distraction from the emotional agony. This act, while providing temporary relief, leaves her with a deeper sense of self-loathing, further cementing her belief that she is damaged and at fault. The avoidance and self-punishment have also made her hypervigilant; by isolating herself, any minor conflict or moment of uncertainty becomes magnified, making the original triggers even more potent. It was after her husband found her crying in the bathroom, staring at the fresh red marks on her arm, that they agreed she needed help. She came to therapy expressing a profound fear that she was permanently broken, but also a fragile hope that she might one day be able to forgive herself.
